Seminar Title:

The Ferritin Iron Cycle from Biomineralization to Mineral Dissolution: Deciphering the Impact of Oxoanions and Thiols

Abstract:

The intricate interplay between iron, sulfur, and oxygen is critical to biology and geochemistry since the evolution of life. The transition from sulfur-rich pre-GOE conditions to oxygen-rich post-GOE environments not only generated an oxidative environment but also hindered iron accessibility, likely driving the evolution of ferritin, a protein cage that detoxifies and stores iron in ferrihydrite form. Upon physiological requirements, ferritin iron is released for cellular metabolic activities and synthesis of Fe-proteins/enzymes. Despite the significance of these thiols, as antioxidants/reducing agents to combat oxidative stress, comprehensive research comparing their interaction with oxidants such as Fe3+/O2, the ability to act as reductants (mineral dissolution from both bare and ferritin encapsulated) and as antioxidants are limited. Interestingly, the native ferritin iron mineral from bacteria/plant contains significant phosphate (oxoanion) content, unlike animals. However, the physiological significance, the cause of this variation and the natural selectivity remain unknown. This dissertation examines both aspects, i.e., how stored iron is mobilized by the thiols and how the oxoanion rich conditions influence the biomineralization in ferritin and the physicochemical aspects of the formed iron mineral.&nbsp

Thiol driven mineral dissolution is influenced by its molecular architecture: size (mineral accessibility), and the number of specific functional groups (-SH, -COO‒ and -NH3+), highlighting entropic contributions (efficacy of dithiols over monothiol). The effectiveness of protein cages and cage type in retaining iron mineral core were established by iron release kinetics. The bare ferrihydrite releasing iron readily than its ferritin-encapsulated counterpart, underscoring the protein cage as a kinetic barrier to reductive dissolution and unveiled the evolutionary upgradation of protein coat. To reveal the significance and selectivity of phosphate over other oxoanions, a set of oxoanion-doped ferritin encapsulated iron mineral (biomineralization) was synthesized. These oxoanion doping differentially influences the O2 utilization, mineral size, crystallinity, and the stability/reactivity towards reductive and non-reductive iron release processes. Moreover, oxoanion identity not only dictates the Fe2+ autoxidation, but also biomineralization in the ferritin cage, influencing the amount of iron loading. Comparison of oxoanion-doped bare and ferritin encapsulated ferrihydrite, ssegregated the protein-cage contribution from oxoanion-iron chemistry and further revealed the structural and kinetic constraints imposed by the protein nanocage. Together, these studies provide a mechanistic foundation for understanding natural iron mineralization and mineral reactivity to meet the physiological iron requirement for the rational design of ferritin-caged iron oxide nanoparticles for environmental (oxoanion-sequestration/photocatalysis) and nutraceutical purpose.
